title: Graph theory basics
summary: A [[graph|graph]] is a set of points, called [[graph-vertex|vertices]], joined by lines, called [[graph-edge|edges]]. It records only what is linked to what, so it can model road maps, circuits, networks and one-way streets. Here you learn the words for describing graphs and how to turn a real situation into one.

goals.text: Describe a graph with the words vertex, edge, adjacent and [[degree-of-a-vertex|degree]], and use the fact that the degrees add up to twice the number of edges.
Represent a real situation, such as a road map or a circuit, as an unweighted or a [[weighted-graph|weighted graph]].
Decide whether a graph is [[simple-graph|simple]], [[complete-graph|complete]] or [[connected-graph|connected]], and give the reason.
Find in-degrees and out-degrees in a [[directed-graph|directed graph]], and decide whether it is [[strongly-connected-graph|strongly connected]].
Identify [[subgraph|subgraphs]] and [[tree|trees]], and use the fact that a tree with $n$ vertices has $n - 1$ edges.

synonyms: what is a tree in graph theory

before.prompt: Six friends meet, and each pair of friends shakes hands once. How many handshakes are there?
before.hint: Count the hands each person shakes, then ask how many times each handshake has been counted.
before.explain: Each of the $6$ friends shakes $5$ hands: $6 \times 5 = 30$. That counts every handshake twice, once for each person in it, so there are $30 \div 2 = 15$.

before.prompt: Bus times are Ashby to Brook $12$ minutes, Ashby to Corfe $25$ minutes and Brook to Corfe $17$ minutes. How long does Ashby to Brook to Corfe take?
before.hint: Add the two legs you actually travel.
before.explain: The route uses Ashby to Brook, then Brook to Corfe: $12 + 17 = 29$ minutes. $25$ is the direct bus, and $42$ adds the direct time to one leg.

blocks.text: A metro map, a ferry network and an office computer network all show some places and which pairs are linked. A graph keeps only that.

blocks.statement: A [[graph|graph]] is a set of [[graph-vertex|vertices]] together with a set of [[graph-edge|edges]]. Each edge joins two vertices, or joins a vertex to itself.
blocks.plain: Dots joined by lines; only the connections matter.

blocks.text: A vertex (plural vertices, or node) is a point. An edge joins two vertices. An edge from a vertex back to itself is a loop. Two or more edges joining the same pair are multiple edges.
Where you draw the vertices, and how long or curved the edges are, means nothing. Edges that cross on paper don't meet unless there is a vertex there.
Two vertices are adjacent if an edge joins them. Two edges are adjacent if they share a vertex.

blocks.statement: The [[degree-of-a-vertex|degree]] of a vertex $V$, written $\deg(V)$, is the number of edge ends at $V$. A loop at $V$ adds $2$ to $\deg(V)$.
blocks.plain: Count the line ends at the dot.

blocks.statement: In every graph, the degrees of all the vertices add up to twice the number of edges.
blocks.why: Each edge has two ends, and each end adds $1$ to a degree.

blocks.text: So the degrees always add to an even number.

blocks.alt: A graph with five vertices A, B, C, D and E. Edges: A to B, A to C, B to C, B to D, two separate edges between C and D, D to E, and a loop at E.
blocks.caption: Trails between five huts. Two trails join C and D; a circular trail starts and ends at E.

blocks.question: For the hut trails in the figure: (a) write down the huts adjacent to B; (b) find the degree of each hut, in the order A, B, C, D, E.
steps: (a) B's edges go to A, C and D, so these are adjacent to B.
(b) A: edges to B and C, so $\deg(\mathrm{A}) = 2$. B: edges to A, C and D, so $\deg(\mathrm{B}) = 3$.
C: edges to A and B, plus two to D, so $\deg(\mathrm{C}) = 4$. D: edges to B and E, plus two to C, so $\deg(\mathrm{D}) = 4$.
E: one edge to D, and the loop adds $2$, so $\deg(\mathrm{E}) = 3$.
Check: there are $8$ edges, and $2 + 3 + 4 + 4 + 3 = 16 = 2 \times 8$.

blocks.question: An office network has $14$ switches. Each switch is cabled directly to exactly $5$ other switches, with at most one cable between any two. Find the number of cables.
steps: Each switch is a vertex of degree $5$, and each cable is an edge.
The degrees add to $14 \times 5 = 70$, which is twice the number of edges.
So there are $70 \div 2 = 35$ cables. In context: $14 \times 5$ counts every cable twice, once at each end.

blocks.prompt: In the hut graph, which pair of edges is adjacent?
blocks.hint: Adjacent edges share a vertex. Look for a letter that appears in both.
blocks.explain: AB and BD share vertex B. The other pairs share no vertex.

blocks.prompt: A graph has $6$ vertices with degrees $1, 2, 2, 3, 3$ and $5$. How many edges does it have?
blocks.explain: The degrees add to $1 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 5 = 16$, which is twice the number of edges. So there are $16 \div 2 = 8$ edges.

blocks.prompt: An engineer wants to link $7$ sensors so that each sensor is joined directly to exactly $3$ others. Which statement is correct?
blocks.hint: Add up what the degrees would be.

options.text: Impossible: the degrees would add to 21, an odd number

blocks.explain: The degrees would add to $7 \times 3 = 21$. A sum of degrees is twice the number of edges, so it must be even.

verify.truth: Impossible: the degrees would add to 21, an odd number

sections.heading: Turning a real situation into a graph

blocks.text: To model a situation, decide what the vertices are (places or objects) and what the edges are (direct links). Leave out real positions and the shapes of roads.
On a map, towns are vertices and roads are edges. In a circuit, junctions are vertices and each component between two junctions is an edge.

blocks.statement: A [[weighted-graph|weighted graph]] is a graph with a number, called a weight, on each edge. Weights usually stand for distances, times or costs.
blocks.plain: Each line says how far, how long or how much.

blocks.text: An unweighted graph only says whether two things are linked. A weighted graph is not drawn to scale, so read the weights, never the line lengths.

blocks.alt: A graph with three vertices P, Q and R. Two separate edges join P and Q, one labelled battery and one labelled bulb. An edge labelled resistor joins P and R, and an edge labelled switch joins R and Q.
blocks.caption: The circuit as a graph.

blocks.question: In a circuit, a battery and a bulb are each connected directly between junctions P and Q. A resistor joins P to a junction R, and a switch joins R to Q. Model the circuit as a graph, and find the degrees of P, Q and R.
steps: Vertices: junctions P, Q and R. Edges: one per component, so $4$ edges.
The battery and bulb both join P and Q: draw two edges between P and Q. The resistor gives PR and the switch gives RQ (see the figure).
P meets the battery, bulb and resistor: $\deg(\mathrm{P}) = 3$. Q meets the battery, bulb and switch: $\deg(\mathrm{Q}) = 3$. R: $\deg(\mathrm{R}) = 2$.
Check: $3 + 3 + 2 = 8 = 2 \times 4$.

blocks.alt: A weighted graph with vertices F, G, H and I. Edge weights: F to G 15, F to H 9, G to H 4, G to I 8, H to I 18, and F to I 24, drawn as a long curve over the top.
blocks.caption: Roads between four villages, in km. Not to scale.

blocks.question: The roads between four villages are: Fenby–Garth $15$ km, Fenby–Holt $9$ km, Garth–Holt $4$ km, Garth–Ince $8$ km, Holt–Ince $18$ km and a mountain road Fenby–Ince $24$ km. (a) Represent the roads as a weighted graph. (b) Find the shortest distance by road from Fenby to Ince.
steps: (a) One vertex per village and one edge per road, labelled with its length (see the figure).
The shortest is $21$ km, via Holt and Garth. In context: the direct mountain road is $3$ km longer than going through two villages.

blocks.prompt: On a weighted graph of roads, edge DS has weight $12$ km and is drawn shorter than edge DT, with weight $7$ km. Which is correct?
blocks.hint: Is a weighted graph drawn to scale?

options.text: The road from D to T is shorter
The road from D to S is shorter
The two roads are the same length

blocks.explain: The weights give the lengths, and $7 < 12$. The drawing is not to scale.

verify.truth: The road from D to T is shorter

blocks.prompt: A rail map shows $6$ stations and the direct lines between them. You model it as a graph. What are the vertices?
blocks.hint: Vertices are the places; edges are the links between them.

options.text: The points where lines cross on the map

blocks.explain: The stations are the vertices and each direct line is an edge. A crossing on the map is not a vertex.

blocks.statement: A [[simple-graph|simple graph]] has no loops and no multiple edges, so each pair of vertices is joined by at most one edge.
A [[complete-graph|complete graph]] is a simple graph in which every pair of distinct vertices is joined by an edge. The complete graph on $n$ vertices is written $K_n$.
blocks.plain: Every dot joined to every other dot, once.

blocks.text: In $K_n$ each vertex has degree $n - 1$, so the degrees add to $n(n - 1)$, and the number of edges is half of that.

blocks.statement: A graph is [[connected-graph|connected]] if you can travel along edges from any vertex to any other vertex.
blocks.plain: The graph is all in one piece.

blocks.text: Every complete graph is connected. A connected graph need not be complete: some pairs may have no direct edge.

blocks.alt: Three graphs. G1: a square A, B, C, D with edges AB, BC, CD, DA and a loop at C. G2: four vertices P, Q, R, S with all six edges, including the two diagonals, which cross without a vertex. G3: a triangle V, W, X and, separately, an edge joining Y and Z.
blocks.caption: Three graphs to classify. In $G_2$ the diagonals cross, but there is no vertex where they cross.

blocks.question: For each graph in the figure, state whether it is simple, connected and complete. Give a reason for each answer.
steps: $G_1$: the loop at C means not simple. The square reaches every vertex, so connected. A and C are not adjacent, so not complete.
$G_2$: no loops or multiple edges, and all $6$ pairs of vertices are joined, so it is complete ($K_4$) and connected.
$G_3$: simple, but there is no route from V to Y, so not connected and not complete.
blocks.answer: $G_1$: not simple (loop at C), connected, not complete. $G_2$: simple, connected and complete ($K_4$). $G_3$: simple, not connected, not complete.

verify.truth: G1 not simple (loop), connected, not complete; G2 is K4; G3 simple, not connected

blocks.question: In a chess tournament, each player plays every other player exactly once. (a) Explain why the games can be modelled by a complete graph, and find the number of games for $16$ players. (b) The hall is booked for at most $100$ games. Use your calculator to find the largest number of players the tournament can take.
steps: (a) Players are vertices and games are edges. Every pair of players meets once, so the graph is $K_{16}$, with $\frac{16 \times 15}{2} = 120$ games.
(b) Write down the condition: $\frac{n(n-1)}{2} \le 100$.
Table of $y = \frac{x(x-1)}{2}$: $x = 14$ gives $91$ and $x = 15$ gives $105$.
$91 \le 100 < 105$, so at most $14$ players. In context: a $15$th player adds $14$ games, going over the limit.

blocks.prompt: A courier firm wants a direct flight route between every pair of its $11$ hubs. How many routes is that?
blocks.hint: The routes form a complete graph. How many edges does $K_{11}$ have?
blocks.explain: $K_{11}$ has $\frac{11 \times 10}{2} = 55$ edges. $11 \times 10$ alone counts each route twice.

blocks.prompt: A graph has vertices A, B, C, D and edges AB, BC and CD only. Which description is correct?
blocks.hint: Can you get from every vertex to every other? Is every pair joined directly?

options.text: Simple and connected, but not complete
Not simple, because A and D are not joined

blocks.explain: No loops or multiple edges: simple. A–B–C–D reaches every vertex: connected. A and D are not adjacent: not complete.

verify.truth: Simple and connected, but not complete

blocks.text: Some links work one way only, like one-way streets. Arrows on the edges record this.

blocks.statement: A [[directed-graph|directed graph]] is a graph in which every edge has a direction, shown by an arrow. An edge directed from A to B can be travelled from A to B only.

blocks.text: A two-way link is drawn as two arrows, one each way.

blocks.statement: The in-degree of a vertex is the number of edges directed into it. The out-degree is the number of edges directed out of it.
In a directed graph, the in-degrees of all the vertices add up to the number of edges, and so do the out-degrees.
blocks.why: Every directed edge leaves exactly one vertex and arrives at exactly one vertex.

blocks.statement: A directed graph is [[strongly-connected-graph|strongly connected]] if, for every pair of vertices A and B, you can travel from A to B and from B to A, following the arrows.
blocks.plain: Everyone can reach everyone, obeying the arrows.

blocks.text: In a directed graph with two or more vertices, a vertex with in-degree $0$ can't be reached, and one with out-degree $0$ is a dead end. Either means the graph is not strongly connected.

blocks.alt: A directed graph with four vertices K, L, M and N. Arrows: K to L, L to M, M to K, L to N, and N to M.
blocks.caption: One-way streets between four junctions.

blocks.question: The figure shows one-way streets between junctions K, L, M and N. Find the in-degree and out-degree of each junction.
steps: The $5$ edges are K→L, L→M, M→K, L→N and N→M.
K: in from M, out to L. L: in from K, out to M and N. M: in from L and N, out to K. N: in from L, out to M.
Check: in-degrees $1 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 5$ and out-degrees $1 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 5$, the number of edges.
blocks.answer: K: in $1$, out $1$; L: in $1$, out $2$; M: in $2$, out $1$; N: in $1$, out $1$.

blocks.question: For the streets in the figure: (a) show that the network is strongly connected; (b) the council reverses the street from K to L, so it now runs from L to K. Determine whether the network is still strongly connected, and interpret your answer.
steps: (a) The route K→L→N→M→K follows the arrows and visits every junction. Going round it, any junction reaches any other.
(b) Now both of K's streets, L→K and M→K, arrive at K, so K has out-degree $0$.
No street leaves K, so the network is not strongly connected. In context: traffic at K would be trapped.
blocks.answer: (a) The route K→L→N→M→K visits every junction, so it is strongly connected. (b) K would have out-degree $0$, so the network is not strongly connected: drivers at K could not leave.

verify.truth: a closed route through all vertices; after reversal K has out-degree 0

blocks.prompt: A directed graph has $5$ vertices and $9$ edges. The out-degrees of four of the vertices are $2, 1, 0$ and $3$. Find the out-degree of the fifth vertex.
blocks.hint: What do all the out-degrees add up to?
blocks.explain: The out-degrees add to the number of edges, $9$. The four given add to $6$, so the fifth is $9 - 6 = 3$.

blocks.prompt: On a social app, an arrow from X to Y means X follows Y. Ana follows Ben and Cara, Ben follows Cara, and Cara follows Ana. Is the “follows” graph strongly connected?
blocks.hint: From each person, try to reach the other two along the arrows.

options.text: Yes: everyone can reach everyone along the arrows
No: Ben does not follow Ana
No: Cara follows only one person

blocks.explain: Ana reaches both directly. Ben reaches Cara, then Ana. Cara reaches Ana, then Ben. Direct arrows are not needed.

verify.truth: Yes: everyone can reach everyone along the arrows

blocks.statement: A [[subgraph|subgraph]] of a graph $G$ is a graph whose vertices and edges all belong to $G$. Every edge in the subgraph must have both of its end vertices in the subgraph.

blocks.text: You may keep a vertex without its edges, but not an edge without its ends, and you can't add new edges.

blocks.alt: A graph G with six vertices A to F. Edges: A to B, A to C, B to C, B to D, C to E, D to E, D to F and E to F.
blocks.caption: Graph $G$, with $6$ vertices and $8$ edges.

blocks.question: For the graph $G$ in the figure, decide which of these are subgraphs of $G$. $H_1$: vertices A, B, C with edges AB and BC. $H_2$: vertices B, D, F with edges BD and BF. $H_3$: vertices D and E with edges DE and EF.
steps: $H_1$: AB and BC are edges of $G$, with both ends kept. It is a subgraph.
$H_2$: BF is not an edge of $G$, so it is not a subgraph.
$H_3$: edge EF is kept but its end F is not, so it is not a subgraph.

blocks.text: A cycle is a closed route along edges back to its start, repeating no edge and no other vertex. A loop, or two edges between the same pair, is already a cycle. Cycles are studied in {{lesson:3.16}}.

blocks.statement: A [[tree|tree]] is a connected graph with no cycles.
blocks.plain: All joined up, with no spare links.

blocks.statement: A tree with $n$ vertices has exactly $n - 1$ edges.
blocks.why: Grow the tree from one vertex: each edge brings in exactly one new vertex, as joining two vertices already reached would make a cycle.

blocks.text: The reverse needs a condition: a graph with $n$ vertices and $n - 1$ edges is a tree only if it is connected.
Trees model networks with no wasted link, such as water pipes. In {{lesson:3.16}} you find the cheapest tree joining every vertex.

blocks.question: A water company plans to link $9$ farms with $8$ pipes. The plan includes pipes PQ, QR and RP between farms P, Q and R. Explain why the plan is not a tree, and what this means for the farms.
steps: P–Q–R–P is a cycle, so the plan is not a tree.
A connected graph with $9$ vertices and $8$ edges is a tree, with no cycle. This plan has a cycle, so it is not connected.
In context: one triangle pipe is spare, and at least one farm is cut off.
blocks.answer: The triangle PQR is a cycle, so the plan is not a tree. With $9$ farms and $8$ pipes it is therefore not connected: at least one farm is cut off.

verify.truth: the triangle is a cycle; 9 vertices and 8 edges with a cycle cannot be connected

blocks.prompt: A tree has $12$ edges. How many vertices does it have?
blocks.hint: A tree with $n$ vertices has $n - 1$ edges.

blocks.prompt: Each graph below has vertices A, B, C and D. Which one is a tree?
blocks.hint: A tree is connected and has no cycle. With $4$ vertices it has $3$ edges.

options.text: Edges AB, BC, CD and DA

blocks.explain: AB, AC, AD is connected with no cycle. AB, BC, CA is a cycle and misses D; AB, BC, CD, DA is a cycle; AB and CD is in two pieces.

blocks.text: Degree counts edge ends at a vertex: a loop adds $2$, and each of several edges between the same two vertices counts.
Weighted graph: each edge carries a distance, time or cost. The drawing is not to scale, so read the weights.
Simple: no loops and no multiple edges. Complete $K_n$: simple, with every pair of its $n$ vertices joined, so it has $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ edges.
Connected: you can travel along edges between any two vertices. Strongly connected (directed graph): you can travel from any vertex to any other following the arrows.
In a directed graph, the in-degrees add up to the number of edges, and so do the out-degrees.
Subgraph: vertices and edges taken from $G$, with both ends of every kept edge also kept.
Tree: connected with no cycles. A tree with $n$ vertices has $n - 1$ edges, and a connected graph with $n$ vertices and $n - 1$ edges is a tree.

mistakes: Counting a loop once. Both ends of a loop are at the same vertex, so it adds $2$ to that vertex's degree.
Calling a connected graph complete. Complete means every pair of vertices is joined directly; connected only needs a route between every pair.
Judging distances from the drawing. Weighted graphs are not to scale, and a route through other vertices can beat a direct edge.
Swapping in-degree and out-degree. In-degree counts arrows arriving at a vertex; out-degree counts arrows leaving it.
Calling a graph a tree from its edge count alone. A graph with $n$ vertices and $n - 1$ edges is a tree only if it is also connected.
Drawing a graph with unlabelled vertices or needless crossings. Label every vertex and avoid crossing edges where you can.
examTips: “Write down the degree”: no working is needed, but count a loop twice and count every edge between the same two vertices.
“State, giving a reason” (simple, connected, complete): name the feature that decides it, such as a loop at C, or a pair of vertices with no edge between them.
“Explain why” a graph is connected but not complete: give both halves. Show a route that reaches every vertex, then name one pair of vertices that are not adjacent.
“Draw” a graph: one labelled vertex per place, one edge per direct link, weights on the edges if they are given, and arrows only for one-way links.
